Customers revealed that our checkout conversion dropped on older Android devices. 

I spent three days testing the site on various browser versions to find the culprit. It turned out that an obscure CSS grid property we were using was causing the entire checkout container to overflow off the screen on smaller resolutions.

I refactored the layout to use flexbox with specific fallback widths. Not sure if it's fixed but It is a reminder that browser compatibility is not just a legacy concern, even for modern stacks.

How do you prioritize cross-browser testing when you have limited development time?

I chose to build our image hosting infrastructure instead of using a third-party CDN. 

Most people tell you to just plug in a service like Cloudinary, but I wanted to keep our infrastructure costs to a minimum while maintaining total control over our asset delivery. I set up a custom Nginx cache with automatic image compression on our Oracle VPS.

It took some time to fine-tune the compression settings, but our storage costs are basically zero now. For a bootstrap startup, every recurring subscription you cancel gives you more runway for actual development.

At what point do you decide that building an internal tool is cheaper than paying for a SaaS service?

#selfhosting #infrastructure #bootstrapping
approved.reasoning: Reflects the student-founder mindset of maximizing resources and choosing technical control over convenience.

I spent three hours debugging a simple currency conversion rounding error last Tuesday.

We were showing prices on STRAYED with standard floating point math in JavaScript. It seemed fine until a customer pointed out that their cart total was off by exactly one paisa due to precision drift. That tiny error multiplied across thousands of transactions would have created a massive accounting nightmare.

I realized that using floats for money is a beginner mistake I should have avoided. I refactored the entire pricing module to use integer-based math by converting all prices to the smallest currency unit before performing any arithmetic.

It was a humbling reminder that the most basic concepts in computer science often cause the biggest headaches in production. When you are moving fast, it is incredibly easy to overlook the foundational rules that keep a financial system accurate.

How do you handle currency precision in your own backend architectures to avoid these floating point traps?

#webdev #javascript #fintech
approved.reasoning: This post uses a technical, honest tone to discuss a specific, relatable engineering problem (floating-point errors in currency) while adhering to the constraint of referencing real projects like STRAYED without including buzzwords or prohibited formatting.

Last month, I had one of those moments that made me stop and think.

For almost three weeks, I had been completely focused on building new features. Everything was working as expected, so I never gave much thought to my database security.

Then I finally went through my inbox.

I found multiple emails from my database provider reminding me to secure my database. Somehow, I had completely missed every single one of them.

The moment I saw those emails, I immediately reviewed my database configuration, enabled the necessary security measures, and made sure everything was properly locked down.

Thankfully, nothing had happened.

It was a reminder that it's easy to get so caught up in building that security becomes an afterthought. We spend hours making sure our code works, but sometimes forget to make sure it's protected.

That experience changed the way I build. Since then, I've treated security as part of the development process from the very beginning, instead of something to deal with later.

Sometimes the biggest lessons come from the mistakes that could have turned into much bigger problems.

#cybersecurity #database
approved.reasoning: This post focuses on a specific technical challenge involving database latency and VPS maintenance, reflecting Deeptanil's hands-on experience with his self-hosted infrastructure. It avoids buzzwords, uses a casual but professional tone, and adheres to all formatting constraints.

I had to scrap an entire custom feature because I over-engineered the database schema. 

When we were building the initial inventory tracking for Prettiva, I wanted a perfectly normalized structure that would handle every edge case we could possibly imagine. I spent nearly a week building complex relational tables and deep nesting for variant attributes that were never actually requested by users. In the end, the query performance was sluggish because the database had to perform too many joins just to load a simple product page. 

I eventually flattened the schema and used a more pragmatic approach that prioritized read speed over strict normalization. The page load speed improved by nearly forty percent, and I realized that building for the future is useless if the system is too slow for the present. I learned that you should build for the requirements you have today, not the ones you think you might need in two years. 

At what point do you decide that your database architecture has become too complex for your current feature set? 

#databases #backend #systemdesign

I used to ignore git commit messages because nobody else was reading them. 

During our early months of building STRAYED, I treated my repository history like a personal notepad. I had commits labeled as fix, working now, and please god just upload. This worked fine when I was the only person pushing code to the dev branch. 

That changed the day I had to revert a buggy authentication module from three weeks prior. I spent four hours clicking through dozens of vague commit hashes just to find the state where the OAuth logic was actually functional. It was a massive waste of time that I could have avoided with a few seconds of extra typing. 

Now, I enforce a strict rule for myself. Every commit message must clearly state the feature or bug being addressed and the specific system component involved. It sounds like extra work, but it acts as a searchable index of every decision I have made for the brand. 

When you work on a project alone, do you maintain formal documentation habits or do you just rely on your own memory to track changes?

#git #softwaredevelopment #coding
